x.ASV: Praise ye Jehovah. Praise, O ye servants of Jehovah, Praise the name of Jehovah.
x.Darby: Hallelujah! Praise, ye servants of Jehovah, praise the name of Jehovah.
x.KJV: Praise ye the Lord. Praise, O ye servants of the Lord, praise the name of the Lord.
x.YLT: Praise ye Jah! Praise, ye servants of Jehovah. Praise the name of Jehovah.

nt: The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

Here, **name** represents who Yahweh is or to refer to Yahweh himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [praise everything about Yahweh]

x.ASV: Blessed be the name of Jehovah From this time forth and for evermore.
x.Darby: Blessed be the name of Jehovah, from this time forth and for evermore!
x.KJV: Blessed be the name of the Lord from this time forth and for evermore.
x.YLT: The name of Jehovah is blessed, From henceforth, and unto the age.

nt: The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. The psalmist is expressing his desire to praise Yahweh. If it would be unnatural to use that form for this purpose, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [We bless Yahweh] or [Let us all praise Yahweh]

The psalmist is referring to all of time by naming two extremes, **now** and **to forever**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [for all eternity]

x.ASV: Jehovah is high above all nations, And his glory above the heavens.
x.Darby: Jehovah is high above all nations, his glory above the heavens.
x.KJV: The Lord is high above all nations, and his glory above the heavens.
x.YLT: High above all nations is Jehovah, Above the heavens is his honour.

nt: Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh as if he were physically **high above** the nations, like someone standing on a mountain looking down. This image emphasizes Yahweh’s supreme authority and power over all earthly kingdoms. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is supreme over all nations]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [his glory is high above the skies]

Here the psalmist is speaking of Yahweh’s **glory** as if it were positioned **above the skies**. The psalmist means that Yahweh’s glory is greater than anything that can be seen in the heavens. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his glory exceeds anything visible from earth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he is more glorious than anything visible from earth]

x.ASV: Who is like unto Jehovah our God, That hath his seat on high,
x.Darby: Who is like unto Jehovah ourGod, who hath placed his dwelling on high;
x.KJV: Who is like unto the Lord our God, who dwelleth on high,
x.YLT: Who is as Jehovah our God, He is exalting Himself to sit?

nt: The psalmist is using the question form for emphasis, which begins here and continues through verse 6. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [There is no one like Yahweh our God]

The psalmist is using **the one making high to sit** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the one who sits on high” or “the one who rules in the highest position.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one sitting on high] or [the one who rules in the highest position]

x.KJV: Who humbleth himself to behold the things that are in heaven, and in the earth!
x.YLT: He is humbling Himself to look On the heavens and on the earth.

nt: This is the second part of the question form that began in verse 5. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for the purpose of creating emphasis as this does, you could translate these two verses as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [the one making low to look on the sky and on the earth.]

The psalmist is using **the one making low to look** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the one who humbles himself to look” or “the one who condescends to look.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one who lowers himself to look down on the sky and on the earth]

x.ASV: He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, And lifteth up the needy from the dunghill;
x.Darby: He raiseth up the poor out of the dust; from the dung-hill he lifteth up the needy,
x.KJV: He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth the needy out of the dunghill;
x.YLT: He is raising up from the dust the poor, From a dunghill He exalteth the needy.

nt: מְקִֽימִ֣י מֵ⁠עָפָ֣ר דָּ֑ל מֵֽ֝⁠אַשְׁפֹּ֗ת יָרִ֥ים אֶבְיֽוֹן

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and you may want to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation. If it is helpful, you could connect the phrases in a way that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [raising up the poor from the dust, yes, he lifts the needy from the garbage]
מְקִֽימִ֣י מֵ⁠עָפָ֣ר דָּ֑ל מֵֽ֝⁠אַשְׁפֹּ֗ת יָרִ֥ים אֶבְיֽוֹן

Here the psalmist is speaking of the extremely poor condition of needy people as if they were sitting in **dust** and **garbage**. If this image communicates well in your language, please use it. If not, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he takes the poor out of their dirty and poor condition]
מְקִֽימִ֣י מֵ⁠עָפָ֣ר דָּ֑ל מֵֽ֝⁠אַשְׁפֹּ֗ת יָרִ֥ים אֶבְיֽוֹן

The psalmist is using the adjectives **poor** and **needy** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [raising up poor people from the dust, he lifts needy people from the garbage]

x.Darby: To set [him] among nobles, among the nobles of his people.
x.KJV: That he may set him with princes, even with the princes of his people.
x.YLT: To cause to sit with princes, With the princes of His people.

nt: The psalmist is using **to seat him with princes** as a common expression of the culture to mean “to give him a position of honor and authority.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to cause him to rule with princes]
The pronoun **him** refers to the poor person mentioned in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [to seat the poor person with princes]

The phrase **with the princes of his people** clarifies who the princes are from the previous phrase. You may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [that is, to seat him with the princes of his people]
Here, **his** could refer to: (1) Yahweh. Alternate translation: [with the princes of Yahweh’s people] or (2) the poor person. Alternate translation: [with the princes of the man’s people]
